challenges.name: keyset-pagination-evidence
challenges.title: Read a keyset page
challenges.description: Two pieces of evidence from the activity feed: the plans of page 1 and of a deep page read with a (created_at, id) cursor, and a page boundary that falls inside a group of events with the same timestamp. Decide whether each statement is true or false.

questions.question:
Index: activity_log_user_created_id ON activity_log (user_id, created_at, id). User 42 has 26,090 events.

-- page 1
Limit  (cost=0.43..21.37 rows=20 width=52) (actual time=0.021..0.044 rows=20 loops=1)
  Buffers: shared hit=5
  ->  Index Scan Backward using activity_log_user_created_id on activity_log  (cost=0.43..27315.12 rows=26090 width=52) (actual time=0.020..0.040 rows=20 loops=1)
        Index Cond: (user_id = 42)
        Buffers: shared hit=5
Execution Time: 0.061 ms

-- a page about 25,000 rows deep, cursor = last row of the previous page
Limit  (cost=0.43..22.01 rows=20 width=52) (actual time=0.025..0.049 rows=20 loops=1)
  Buffers: shared hit=6
  ->  Index Scan Backward using activity_log_user_created_id on activity_log  (cost=0.43..1210.42 rows=1121 width=52) (actual time=0.024..0.045 rows=20 loops=1)
        Index Cond: ((user_id = 42) AND (ROW(created_at, id) < ROW('2025-11-03 18:22:41.512+00'::timestamp with time zone, 77012345)))
        Buffers: shared hit=6
Execution Time: 0.068 ms

Statement: "The deep page touches about as many buffers as page 1 because the index scan starts at the cursor instead of walking past the rows of the earlier pages."
questions.explanation: True. The row comparison is an Index Cond, not a Filter: the B-tree descends directly to the position of (42, '2025-11-03 18:22:41.512', 77012345) and reads backward from there. Both pages read 20 rows and 5-6 buffers, and both stop as soon as Limit has its 20 rows. The common misconception is that a deep page must cost more because "the database has to find where page 1250 starts". With OFFSET it does; with a keyset cursor the position is a key the index can seek to. Check it the same way: compare actual rows and Buffers of page 1 and of a deep page.

questions.question:
Completing a lesson inserts three events in one transaction, so they share created_at (now() is the start time of the transaction).

SELECT id, kind FROM activity_log
WHERE user_id = 42 AND created_at = '2026-10-24 14:03:17.25+00' ORDER BY id DESC;

   id    |      kind
---------+-----------------
 8812043 | streak_extended
 8812042 | lesson_completed
 8812041 | badge_earned

Page 1 (LIMIT 20, ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC) ended with the row 8812042. The feed then requests page 2:

SELECT id, kind, created_at FROM activity_log
WHERE user_id = 42 AND created_at < '2026-10-24 14:03:17.25+00'
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20;

Statement: "Because ORDER BY ends with id as a tie-breaker, page 2 starts with the row 8812041."
questions.explanation: False. ORDER BY only decides the order of the rows that pass WHERE. The cursor condition created_at < '...17.25' excludes every row with exactly that timestamp, so 8812041 (badge_earned) is never shown on any page: the feed silently loses the rows of a tie group that did not fit on the previous page. The cursor has to carry the tie-breaker too: (created_at, id) < ('2026-10-24 14:03:17.25+00', 8812042). The common misconception is that a unique ORDER BY is enough; the WHERE of the next page must use the same columns as the ORDER BY.

challenges.name: activity-feed-keyset-page
challenges.title: Keyset pagination for the activity feed
challenges.description: The activity feed on a CodeDev profile loads newest first with infinite scroll, and events go missing: a lesson completion writes three events in one transaction with the same created_at, and the old cursor (created_at < the last created_at) skipped the ones that did not fit on the previous page. Write NEXT_PAGE, the SQL for the page after a given last row. Table: activity_log(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, user_id, kind, created_at TEXT 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS'); created_at is not unique and ids are not in time order (imported events got larger ids with their original timestamps). The runner creates the index activity_log_user_created_id ON activity_log (user_id, created_at, id). NEXT_PAGE gets the named parameters :user_id, :last_created_at, :last_id (the last row of the previous page) and :limit, and returns id, kind, created_at of the next :limit rows of that user in the order created_at DESC, id DESC, so that every row appears exactly once across all pages. Do not use OFFSET: each page must be read through the index starting at the cursor. SQLite has supported row values like (a, b) < (?, ?) since 3.15, with the same tuple comparison as PostgreSQL. The test runner at the bottom of the file runs FIRST_PAGE (given), then NEXT_PAGE with the last row of each page until a page has fewer than :limit rows, with a budget of SQLite VM steps per page (a page that reads far more rows than it returns is stopped as "too slow"), checks with EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN that NEXT_PAGE uses activity_log_user_created_id without a temporary B-tree for sorting, and prints {"pages": <pages read>, "ids": [<ids in feed order>], "plan": "ok"}.
hints: The next page must contain the rows that come after the last row in the order created_at DESC, id DESC. Which rows with exactly the same created_at as the last row still belong on the next page?

Look at the columns of ORDER BY and the columns of your cursor condition: they must be the same, in the same order and direction. Then look at how the condition uses created_at: the index can only seek on the column itself, not on an expression computed from it.

A similar case on other data: a leaderboard ordered by score DESC, user_id DESC, where the last row shown was (score 870, user_id 31). The next page is WHERE (score, user_id) < (870, 31) ORDER BY score DESC, user_id DESC LIMIT 10. It keeps (870, 12), which a cursor of score < 870 would skip, and it never returns (870, 31) or (870, 45) again.

tests.name: Example: three events in one second split across pages, none skipped
Imported events: large ids with old timestamps stay in time order
A whole page of rows with the same timestamp
Rows of other users with the same timestamps never appear
Exactly two full pages: the third page is empty
Invalid input: an unknown user id gets one empty page
Large: 3,000 events of one user in pages of 25 within the per-page budget
